clinicalPearls: Presents as multiple small, smooth, dark brown to black dome-shaped papules on the face, especially the malar region and periorbital skin.
It is regarded as a variant of seborrhoeic keratosis occurring predominantly in people of African and, less commonly, Asian descent.
Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood, with lesions increasing in number and size over time.
There is a strong familial tendency and a female predominance, and lesions are entirely benign.
The papules are asymptomatic and of cosmetic concern only, though occasional lesions may become pruritic or catch on clothing.
Diagnosis is clinical; dermoscopy shows features shared with seborrhoeic keratosis such as comedo-like openings and a cerebriform pattern.
Treatment is for cosmetic reasons and includes light electrodesiccation, curettage, snip excision or laser, undertaken cautiously given the risk of dyspigmentation.
Careful test treatment of a few lesions is advised in richly pigmented skin because of the risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and keloid scarring.
reference.pathophysiology: Dermatosis papulosa nigra is considered a clinical variant of seborrhoeic keratosis, with histology showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and elongation of rete ridges in an epidermal proliferation of basaloid and squamoid keratinocytes. A pronounced familial and genetic predisposition in people with darker skin phototypes underlies the characteristic distribution and early onset, and a naevoid or developmental defect of the pilosebaceous follicle has been proposed. Increased epidermal melanisation accounts for the dark colour. As with seborrhoeic keratosis, the lesions are benign proliferations without malignant potential.

reference.prognosis: Dermatosis papulosa nigra is entirely benign with no malignant potential; lesions persist and slowly accumulate over life. Cosmetic treatment can improve appearance but carries a risk of dyspigmentation and scarring in richly pigmented skin.
pitfalls: Aggressive or extensive destructive treatment causing post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation or keloid scarring in darker skin.
Failing to perform a test treatment before treating numerous lesions.
Overlooking an atypical lesion within the field that warrants biopsy.
Confusing the condition with flat warts and applying inappropriate therapy.
management: Reassure that the lesions are entirely benign with no malignant potential and that treatment is purely cosmetic
Make the diagnosis clinically and dermoscopically, reserving biopsy for atypical lesions
Offer cosmetic removal of troublesome lesions by light electrodesiccation, curettage, scissor snip, cryotherapy or laser
Perform test-spot treatment first to gauge the pigmentary response before treating widely, given the risk of dyspigmentation in richly pigmented skin
Use gentle technique and photoprotection to minimise post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and scarring
Use clinical photography to monitor cosmetic treatment outcomes
